nodes.title: Tokens: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Tokens. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: What is the fundamental identity object returned by ALL Vault auth methods after?
flashcards.back: All Vault auth methods (AppRole, LDAP, Kubernetes, AWS, etc.) return a Vault token after successful authentication. The token has attached policies, a TTL, and an accessor. It is the core identity mechanism used for all subsequent API calls.

flashcards.front: A high-throughput application creates thousands of Vault tokens per second. Whic?
flashcards.back: Batch tokens are encoded entirely in the token string and not stored in Vault's storage backend. This makes them extremely lightweight — no storage write per token creation. They cannot be renewed and have no children, but for short-lived, high-volume use cases (Lambda functions, CI/CD jobs) they are far more efficient than service tokens. and faster to create

flashcards.front: A Vault token has a TTL of 1 hour but the application needs it to remain valid f?
flashcards.back: Vault tokens with 'renewable: true' can be renewed before expiry using vault token renew (or the API equivalent). Each renewal extends the TTL by its increment, but the token cannot be renewed past max_ttl. Vault Agent automates this for applications. Setting TTL to 0 does NOT make a token immortal — it uses the system default TTL.

flashcards.front: What is the 'orphan' flag on a Vault token?
flashcards.back: Normally, revoking a parent token revokes all its child tokens. An orphan token (token_type = orphan) has no parent — it exists independently. This is important for long-running services that authenticate via AppRole: the AppRole login token is ephemeral (parent), but the service shouldn't lose access just because the login token expired. Orphan tokens persist until their own TTL expires or they're explicitly revoked. it survives independently of the creating token's lifecycle

nodes.title: Mixed Topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Mixed Topics. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: What are the capabilities that a Vault policy can grant on a path?
flashcards.back: Vault policy capabilities: create (write new), read, update (overwrite existing), delete, list (enumerate keys), sudo (root-restricted operations), deny (explicit deny overrides any allow). Policies are written in HCL or JSON and assigned to tokens at authentication time.

flashcards.front: A Vault policy contains path 'secret/data/app/*' { capabilities = ['read'] }. Wh?
flashcards.back: The policy grants only 'read' capability on the path. Writing (vault kv put) requires 'create' or 'update' capability. Listing requires 'list' capability on the parent path. The policy explicitly restricts writes, so vault kv put would be denied. Note: list also requires listing the path secret/metadata/app/ for KV v2.

flashcards.front: A team wants to create a Vault policy that allows listing secrets in secret/team?
flashcards.back: In KV v2, listing secrets requires 'list' on 'secret/metadata/team-a/*'. Reading secret values requires 'read' on 'secret/data/team-a/*'. By granting list on the metadata path only (without read on data), users can see secret names but cannot read their values. This separation is a KV v2 advantage over v1.

flashcards.front: What does the 'default' policy in Vault contain and when is it applied?
flashcards.back: The 'default' policy is automatically attached to every token created in Vault. It grants minimal permissions like token renewal (auth/token/renew-self), self-lookup (auth/token/lookup-self), and revocation (auth/token/revoke-self). You can add more permissions to the default policy or explicitly exclude it using token_no_default_policy in auth roles. self-lookup) — attached to ALL tokens automatically
